questionText: Beekeeping is said to create a positive externality of production. What does this mean?
answers: When beekeepers produce honey, their bees pollinate neighbouring orchards, benefiting farmers who did not pay for it.
When people consume honey, they become healthier, benefiting the wider community.
Honey is expensive to produce, so beekeepers earn high profits.
Producing honey creates pollution that harms nearby residents.

questionText: Why is the benefit from beekeeping described as an externality of production rather than of consumption?
answers: Because the extra benefit arises from the act of producing honey (the bees pollinating crops), not from anyone consuming it.
Because only producers, not consumers, are allowed to keep bees.
Because honey is consumed by producers themselves.
Because the government pays a subsidy to honey producers.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Three curves are labelled on the diagram. What do the abbreviations MPC, MSC and MSB stand for?
answers: Maximum private cost, maximum social cost and maximum social benefit.
Marginal private cost, marginal social cost and marginal social benefit.
Market price cost, market supply cost and market social benefit.
Mean private cost, mean social cost and mean social benefit.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Which curve shows the true cost to society of producing each tonne of honey?
answers: MPC, because it shows the cost the beekeeper personally pays.
MSB, because it shows the benefit society receives from honey.
MSC, because it lies below MPC once the external benefit of pollination is subtracted from the private cost.
Neither curve, because external benefits cannot be shown on a diagram.

title: Market for honey
questionText: At every quantity, MSC lies $20 below MPC. What does this vertical gap of $20 measure?
answers: The marginal external benefit — the value the pollination gives to farmers other than the beekeeper.
The marginal private cost paid by the beekeeper.
The marginal social benefit consumers receive from honey.
The profit the beekeeper makes on each tonne.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Beekeepers decide how much honey to produce by weighing up their own private costs. What quantity does the free market produce?
answers: 60 tonnes, where demand meets MSC.
50 tonnes, where demand meets MPC.
40 tonnes, where MPC meets MSC.
70 tonnes, where demand meets the horizontal axis.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Society should produce honey up to the point where the benefit to society equals the true cost to society. Compared with the socially optimal quantity, the free market:
answers: Over-produces by 10 tonnes, producing 60 tonnes rather than 50 tonnes.
Under-produces by 10 tonnes, producing 50 tonnes rather than 60 tonnes.
Produces exactly the socially optimal quantity of 50 tonnes.
Under-produces by 20 tonnes, producing 50 tonnes rather than 70 tonnes.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Left to market forces alone, only 50 tonnes of honey are produced instead of the socially optimal 60 tonnes. At the market quantity, MSB (the demand curve) is $50 while MSC is only $30. What deadweight loss does the unregulated market create?
answers: $20 million, calculated as 10 tonnes × $20.
$500, calculated as 50 tonnes × $10.
$50, calculated as ½ × 10 tonnes × $10.
$100, calculated as ½ × 10 tonnes × $20.

title: Market for honey
questionText: Because this is a positive externality of production, the government pays beekeepers a per-unit subsidy to move the market to the socially optimal 60 tonnes. How large must the subsidy be, and who receives it?
answers: A subsidy of $20 per tonne, paid to consumers, who then pay $30 for honey.
A subsidy of $10 per tonne, paid to beekeepers, who then receive $50.
A subsidy of $20 per tonne, paid to beekeepers; consumers pay $40 and beekeepers receive $60.
A subsidy of $60 per tonne, paid to beekeepers, who then supply honey for free.
